VIDEO.title: Why Romans 8 Doesn't Always Feel True
VIDEO.series: The Book of Romans, Every Word (playlist of 28 videos)

kicker: Study aid · Romans 8:31-39 · Episode 15 (#15 of 28 in the playlist)
SUMMARY: The teacher opens with a question: what if you believe God loves you but still don't feel safe with Him? He reads Romans 8:31-39. If God is for us, who is against us (8:31)? He who did not spare His own Son will graciously give us all things (8:32). Who will bring a charge against God's elect? God is the one who justifies (8:33). Christ died, was raised and intercedes for us (8:34). No affliction, persecution or sword can separate us from the love of Christ (8:35-36); in all these things we overwhelmingly conquer (8:37), and nothing in all creation can separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord (8:38-39).

Paul is concluding a train of thought that began in Romans 1:16: God's righteousness, His covenant faithfulness, is revealed in the gospel. 'What then shall we say to these things?' (8:31) asks for the logical conclusion of everything since chapter 1. Verse 32 is a kal vachomer, arguing from lesser to greater, as in Romans 5:9-10, 15 and 17.

Romans 8:33 uses 'elect' for the first time in the letter and ties it to justification. Paul has been circling election language: the Jews entrusted with the oracles of God (3:1-2), Abraham the father of many nations before Torah (4:17), corporate identity in Adam and in Christ (5-6), sons and heirs (8:29-30, which some, like John Piper, call 'the golden chain'). Why wait this long to use the word? The teacher asks viewers for their thoughts.

Every rhetorical question has the same answer: no one and nothing. Being more than conquerors (the LSB has 'we overwhelmingly conquer', 8:37) flags a unique battle: sin, persecution and death are not removed from the battlefield, but by remaining faithful and abiding in the Son, Christians render them powerless to separate us from Him. Suffering becomes the context in which God displays His covenant faithfulness.

Old Testament background: 'Yahweh is for me' (Psalm 118:6) and 'Who is he who condemns Me?' (Isaiah 50:8-9); the heavenly courtroom of Zechariah 3:1-4, where Yahweh rebukes Satan and clothes Joshua the high priest; the reigning King (Psalm 110:1) who is also the interceding Servant (Isaiah 53:12); the covenant curses (Deuteronomy 28:15-68) behind the list in 8:35; and Psalm 44:22, a lament of a faithful people who still suffer. A list of election themes follows, as preparation for Romans 9.

Background: after Claudius expelled the Jews from Rome in 49, the church became predominantly Gentile. Returning Jewish believers, and non-Messianic Torah-observant Jews, likely said of the Gentile Christians: they claim Israel's Messiah but don't live like Israel. The verse of the week is 8:33. The lesson: 'God alone determines who belongs to him. And he does so by his justification, not by human performance.'
QUOTES: God alone determines who belongs to him. And he does so by his justification, not by human performance.
By remaining faithful to God and abiding in the Son, Christians render these enemies completely powerless.
The entire letter has been one long response to covenant accusations.
Our belonging is anchored in his love, not our performance.

method.p: Read Romans 8:31-39 and list every question Paul asks (8:31, 32, 33, 34, 35). Beside each, write Paul's answer in one word, then the reason he gives. Which reason rests on what God has done, and which on what we do?

LSB_QUOTES.text: What then shall we say to these things? If God is for us, who is against us?
Who will bring a charge against God’s elect? God is the one who justifies;
But in all these things we overwhelmingly conquer through Him who loved us.

src.text: What then shall we say to these things? If God is for us, who is against us?

lines.text: 'These things' are everything Paul has said since Romans 1, in response to the clash inside the church in Rome. Paul began by saying he is not ashamed of the gospel, because in it God's righteousness, His covenant faithfulness, is revealed (1:16-17).
The gospel is not merely a message about how to get saved but the announcement that God's reign has broken in.

left.text: Yahweh is for me; I will not fear; / What can man do to me?

right.text: He who vindicates Me is near; / Who will contend with Me? / Let us stand up to each other; / Who has a judgment against Me? / Let him approach Me. / Behold, Lord Yahweh helps Me; / Who is he who condemns Me?

lines.text: 'If God is for us' is covenant assurance language, spoken about Yahweh before. Isaiah's string of courtroom questions sounds very like Paul's in 8:33-34.

left.text: He who indeed did not spare His own Son, but delivered Him over for us all, how will He not also with Him graciously give us all things?

right.text: For if while we were enemies we were reconciled to God through the death of His Son, much more, having been reconciled, we shall be saved by His life.

lines.text: Kal vachomer, a rabbinic way of teaching, argues from the lesser to the greater: if something is true on a smaller scale, it is certainly true on a larger one. Paul used it in Romans 5:9-10, 15 and 17.
Study note (added): 'did not spare His own Son' echoes Genesis 22:16, 'have not spared your son, your only one'; the Greek Old Testament uses the same verb for 'spare' there.

src.text: Who will bring a charge against God’s elect? God is the one who justifies;

lines.text: Paul uses 'elect' here for the first time and ties it to justification. But he has been circling election language: the Jews entrusted with the oracles of God (3:2), Abraham the father of many nations before Torah (4:17), corporate identity in Adam and in Christ (chapters 5-6), and sons and heirs (8:14-17, 29-30).
Paul refrains from the word until he has shown who God's people are (in Christ), how they got there (the Spirit, adoption, union) and what secures them: God's action, not theirs.

left.text: Then he showed me Joshua the high priest standing before the angel of Yahweh, and Satan standing at his right hand to accuse him. And Yahweh said to Satan, “Yahweh rebuke you, Satan! Indeed, Yahweh who has chosen Jerusalem rebuke you! Is this not a brand delivered from the fire?”

right.text: And he answered and spoke to those who were standing before him, saying, “Remove the filthy garments from him.” Again he said to him, “See, I have made your iniquity pass away from you and will clothe you with festal robes.”

lines.text: Joshua represents God's elect people Israel. Satan stands ready to accuse, but the Lord silences him and declares Joshua acquitted before any defense is offered. Note 'chosen' (election) and the removal of iniquity and new clothing (justification). The teacher believes Paul has this passage in mind in 8:33.
Study note (added): Revelation 12:10 calls Satan 'the accuser of our brothers', 'thrown down'.

left.text: who is the one who condemns? Christ Jesus is He who died, yes, rather who was raised, who is at the right hand of God, who also intercedes for us.

right.text: Because He poured out His soul to death, / And was numbered with the transgressors; / Yet He Himself bore the sin of many, / And interceded for the transgressors.

lines.text: This draws on Psalm 110:1, Isaiah 53:12 and Daniel 7:13-14. Jesus is both reigning King (Psalm 110) and the Servant who intercedes (Isaiah 53): He rules the world while advocating for us within God's covenant.
Study note (added): 'He always lives to make intercession for them' (Hebrews 7:25); 'we have an Advocate with the Father' (1 John 2:1).

left.text: Who will separate us from the love of Christ? Will affliction, or turmoil, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or peril, or sword?

right.text: therefore you shall serve your enemies whom Yahweh will send against you, in hunger, in thirst, in nakedness, and in the lack of all things; and He will put an iron yoke on your neck until He has destroyed you.

lines.text: Israel was promised covenant curses for disobedience (Deuteronomy 28:15-68), and the maladies listed there track the categories in Romans 8:35. 'That's not an accident.' Why does Paul stress that no suffering can separate them from Christ? The teacher asks viewers to infer it.
Study note (added): Deuteronomy 28 names hunger and nakedness (28:48), the sword (28:22) and siege distress (28:53).

left.text: All this has come upon us, but we have not forgotten You, / And we have not dealt falsely with Your covenant.

right.text: But for Your sake we are killed all day long; / We are counted as sheep for the slaughter.

lines.text: Paul quotes Psalm 44:22 directly. In this lament the people of God have not forsaken Yahweh, yet they still suffer. Paul is proving a point about God and suffering: suffering is not a sign of being outside the covenant.

src.text: But in all these things we overwhelmingly conquer through Him who loved us. For I am convinced that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor rulers, nor things present, nor things to come, nor powers, nor height, nor depth, nor any other created thing, will be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord.

lines.text: Why 'more than conquerors'? Our enemies (sin, persecution, death) are not removed from the battlefield as in ordinary war. By remaining faithful and abiding in the Son, Christians render them powerless to accomplish their goal of separating us from Him.
Suffering does not merely fail to defeat Christians; it becomes the context in which God displays His covenant faithfulness to the world.

BACKGROUND.p: Zechariah prophesied in 520 BC, after the return from Babylonian exile, as the temple was being rebuilt (Zechariah 1:1; Ezra 5:1). Joshua the high priest and Zerubbabel the governor led the community (Haggai 1:1). A returned remnant, 'a brand delivered from the fire,' needed assurance that God still claimed them.
The phrase is older than modern preachers: the English Puritan William Perkins titled a 1591 book 'A Golden Chain', laying out the order of salvation drawn from texts like Romans 8:29-30.

Around AD 49 Claudius expelled Jews from Rome (Acts 18:2). The video suggests returning Jewish believers found Gentile-led churches and that non-Messianic Jews may also have pressed the charge 'they claim Israel's Messiah but don't live like Israel.' This is a reconstruction; Romans itself shows disputes over food and days (Romans 14-15).

DEBATES.p: Reformed readers see God's choice of individuals to salvation; Arminian readers tie election to foreseen faith; others, like the video, stress corporate and covenant election drawn from Israel (Deuteronomy 7:6), with individuals included in Christ. Romans 9-11 is where the debate continues.
Some take it as ongoing pleading before the Father (Hebrews 7:25); others, like Chrysostom, read it as human language for His continuing love and advocacy based on His finished work.

DEBATES.h: Who were the accusers in Rome?
DEBATES.p: The video proposes pressure from non-Messianic Torah-observant Jews as well as tensions inside the church. Others see the conflict as mainly internal. The letter does not name outside accusers.

CAREFUL_INTRO: Small slips worth knowing (offered gently; the video's main points stand):
CAREFUL: At about 20:05 the video says Christians with a Gentile background were urging Jewish believers to keep the works of the law. From the rest of the series, the teacher seems to mean the reverse (Jewish-background believers urging Gentiles); it is likely a slip of the tongue.
'More than conquerors' is the video's translation; the LSB reads 'we overwhelmingly conquer' (one Greek verb, hypernikaō).
The video reads 'Who shall separate us… tribulation or distress… danger'; the LSB has 'affliction, or turmoil… peril'.
The video's Zechariah 3:4 reads 'I have taken your iniquity away… pure vestments'; the LSB has 'I have made your iniquity pass away from you and will clothe you with festal robes.'

QUESTIONS: Do you believe God loves you but still not feel safe with Him? What do you think is underneath that?
Why do you think Paul waits until 8:33 to use the word 'elect'?
What accusations, from others or from yourself, does 'God is the one who justifies' answer?
How is being 'more than conquerors' different from having no enemies?
Where do you slip into an employer-employee relationship with God?
APPLICATION_VIDEO: The teacher shares that he grew up with an often cold and distant father with a hot temper; he rarely felt secure and felt he had to perform to belong. Tim Keller notes many treat God like an employer: perform and keep performing in order to belong. That is unbiblical and spiritually dangerous, and it is what Paul corrects in Rome. It turns us into Pharisees; the teacher calls it his own struggle, like Martha refusing to sit at Jesus' feet. Nothing can earn our place; Jesus bore our sins and God counts His righteousness to us. Our belonging is anchored in His love, so what we do for God comes from gratitude: not sitting on the sidelines, which makes grace cheap, and not thinking our ministry earns our standing, which leads to pride, hypocrisy and Pharisaism.
APPLICATION_ADDED: Study note (added): write down one thing you do for God that you secretly count on to make you belong. This week, do it once purely as thanks, and spend the same amount of time simply sitting with Romans 8:31-39.

   (video) Joshua represents God's elect people Israel. Satan stands ready to accuse, but the Lord silences him and declares Joshua acquitted before any defense is offered. Note 'chosen' (election) and the removal of iniquity and new clothing (justification). The teacher believes Paul has this passage in mind in 8:33.
   [Background] Study note (added): Revelation 12:10 calls Satan 'the accuser of our brothers', 'thrown down'. (Revelation 12:10)
3. Romans 8:34; Isaiah 53:12; Psalm 110:1: King and intercessor
   Paul (Romans 8:34, LSB): "who is the one who condemns? Christ Jesus is He who died, yes, rather who was raised, who is at the right hand of God, who also intercedes for us."
   Isaiah (Isaiah 53:12, LSB): "Because He poured out His soul to death, / And was numbered with the transgressors; / Yet He Himself bore the sin of many, / And interceded for the transgressors."
   (video) This draws on Psalm 110:1, Isaiah 53:12 and Daniel 7:13-14. Jesus is both reigning King (Psalm 110) and the Servant who intercedes (Isaiah 53): He rules the world while advocating for us within God's covenant. (Psalm 110:1; Daniel 7:13-14)
   [Background] Study note (added): 'He always lives to make intercession for them' (Hebrews 7:25); 'we have an Advocate with the Father' (1 John 2:1). (Hebrews 7:25; 1 John 2:1)

## Who will separate us?
1. Romans 8:35; Deuteronomy 28: The list of troubles
   Paul (Romans 8:35, LSB): "Who will separate us from the love of Christ? Will affliction, or turmoil, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or peril, or sword?"
   Moses (Deuteronomy 28:48, LSB): "therefore you shall serve your enemies whom Yahweh will send against you, in hunger, in thirst, in nakedness, and in the lack of all things; and He will put an iron yoke on your neck until He has destroyed you."
   (video) Israel was promised covenant curses for disobedience (Deuteronomy 28:15-68), and the maladies listed there track the categories in Romans 8:35. 'That's not an accident.' Why does Paul stress that no suffering can separate them from Christ? The teacher asks viewers to infer it.
   [Background] Study note (added): Deuteronomy 28 names hunger and nakedness (28:48), the sword (28:22) and siege distress (28:53). (Deuteronomy 28:22; Deuteronomy 28:53)
2. Psalm 44:17, 22; Romans 8:36: Sheep for the slaughter
   Psalm 44 (Psalm 44:17, LSB): "All this has come upon us, but we have not forgotten You, / And we have not dealt falsely with Your covenant."
   Psalm 44 (Psalm 44:22, LSB): "But for Your sake we are killed all day long; / We are counted as sheep for the slaughter."
   (video) Paul quotes Psalm 44:22 directly. In this lament the people of God have not forsaken Yahweh, yet they still suffer. Paul is proving a point about God and suffering: suffering is not a sign of being outside the covenant.
3. Romans 8:37-39: More than conquerors
   Rendered powerless Romans 8:37-39: "But in all these things we overwhelmingly conquer through Him who loved us. For I am convinced that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor rulers, nor things present, nor things to come, nor powers, nor height, nor depth, nor any other created thing, will be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord." https://read.lsbible.org/?q=Romans+8:37-39
   (video) Why 'more than conquerors'? Our enemies (sin, persecution, death) are not removed from the battlefield as in ordinary war. By remaining faithful and abiding in the Son, Christians render them powerless to accomplish their goal of separating us from Him.
   (video) Suffering does not merely fail to defeat Christians; it becomes the context in which God displays His covenant faithfulness to the world.

## Key people
- Paul: Concludes the argument begun in Romans 1 with questions whose answer is always no one and nothing. [Background] He wrote Romans probably from Corinth, before taking the collection to Jerusalem (Romans 15:25-26).
- Joshua the high priest: Represents God's elect people in Zechariah's vision; accused by Satan, acquitted and clothed (Zechariah 3:1-4). [Background] High priest after the return from exile, alongside Zerubbabel (Haggai 1:1). Not Joshua son of Nun.
- Satan: Stands at Joshua's right hand to accuse him and is rebuked by Yahweh (Zechariah 3:1-2). [Background] Hebrew satan means 'adversary, accuser'.
- Claudius: Expelled the Jews from Rome in AD 49, leaving a predominantly Gentile church. [Background] Roman emperor AD 41-54; the expulsion is mentioned in Acts 18:2.
- Martha and Mary: Martha refused to sit at Jesus' feet when it mattered: a picture of performing for God instead of being with Him. [Background] 'Mary has chosen the good part, which shall not be taken away from her' (Luke 10:42).
- Tim Keller: Cited: many treat their relationship with God as employer and employee, performing in order to belong. [Background] New York pastor and author (1950-2023).
- John Piper: Cited as one who calls Romans 8:29-30 the golden chain. [Background] American pastor and author.

## Places [Background]
- Rome (named in the video): Jews expelled in 49; Jewish believers later returned to a mostly Gentile church.
- Jerusalem (named in the video): 'Yahweh who has chosen Jerusalem rebuke you' (Zechariah 3:2).
- Corinth: Where Paul probably wrote Romans.
- Bethany: Home of Martha and Mary (John 11:1); Luke 10:38 says only 'a village'.

## Key terms
- Kal vachomer: Rabbinic argument from the lesser to the greater (Romans 8:32; 5:9-10).
- Elect: Chosen by God; first used in Romans at 8:33 and tied to justification.
- Golden chain: A name for Romans 8:29-30: foreknew, predestined, called, justified, glorified.
- Intercede: To plead on another's behalf; Christ at the right hand (8:34).
- Covenant curses: Consequences promised for Israel's disobedience (Deuteronomy 28:15-68).
- Lament: A prayer of complaint and trust in suffering, like Psalm 44.
- Mitzvot ma'asei haTorah: The video's Hebrew for 'works of the law'.
- Pharisaism: In the video: performing for God to earn standing, leading to pride and hypocrisy.

## Historical and cultural background [Background: established]
- Zechariah's setting: Zechariah prophesied in 520 BC, after the return from Babylonian exile, as the temple was being rebuilt (Zechariah 1:1; Ezra 5:1). Joshua the high priest and Zerubbabel the governor led the community (Haggai 1:1). A returned remnant, 'a brand delivered from the fire,' needed assurance that God still claimed them.
- The 'golden chain': The phrase is older than modern preachers: the English Puritan William Perkins titled a 1591 book 'A Golden Chain', laying out the order of salvation drawn from texts like Romans 8:29-30.
- Accusations in Rome: Around AD 49 Claudius expelled Jews from Rome (Acts 18:2). The video suggests returning Jewish believers found Gentile-led churches and that non-Messianic Jews may also have pressed the charge 'they claim Israel's Messiah but don't live like Israel.' This is a reconstruction; Romans itself shows disputes over food and days (Romans 14-15).

- John Chrysostom (c. AD 391): "For when the Judge's sentence declares us just, and a Judge such as that too, what signifies the accuser?" Homilies on Romans 15, on 8:33-34. NPNF 1.11 (public domain).
- John Chrysostom (c. AD 391): "For what is indeed wonderful is this, not that we are conquerors only, but that we are so by the very things meant as plots against us." Homilies on Romans 15, on 8:37. NPNF 1.11 (public domain).

## Where scholars differ [Background: debated]
- Elect: individuals or a people? (8:33) Reformed readers see God's choice of individuals to salvation; Arminian readers tie election to foreseen faith; others, like the video, stress corporate and covenant election drawn from Israel (Deuteronomy 7:6), with individuals included in Christ. Romans 9-11 is where the debate continues.
- Does Christ still 'intercede'? (8:34) Some take it as ongoing pleading before the Father (Hebrews 7:25); others, like Chrysostom, read it as human language for His continuing love and advocacy based on His finished work.
- Who were the accusers in Rome? The video proposes pressure from non-Messianic Torah-observant Jews as well as tensions inside the church. Others see the conflict as mainly internal. The letter does not name outside accusers.

## Careful reading notes
Small slips worth knowing (offered gently; the video's main points stand):
- At about 20:05 the video says Christians with a Gentile background were urging Jewish believers to keep the works of the law. From the rest of the series, the teacher seems to mean the reverse (Jewish-background believers urging Gentiles); it is likely a slip of the tongue.
- 'More than conquerors' is the video's translation; the LSB reads 'we overwhelmingly conquer' (one Greek verb, hypernikaō).
- The video reads 'Who shall separate us… tribulation or distress… danger'; the LSB has 'affliction, or turmoil… peril'.
- The video's Zechariah 3:4 reads 'I have taken your iniquity away… pure vestments'; the LSB has 'I have made your iniquity pass away from you and will clothe you with festal robes.'

## Reflection and discussion questions
1. Do you believe God loves you but still not feel safe with Him? What do you think is underneath that?
2. Why do you think Paul waits until 8:33 to use the word 'elect'?
3. What accusations, from others or from yourself, does 'God is the one who justifies' answer?
4. How is being 'more than conquerors' different from having no enemies?
5. Where do you slip into an employer-employee relationship with God?

## Application
- (video) The teacher shares that he grew up with an often cold and distant father with a hot temper; he rarely felt secure and felt he had to perform to belong. Tim Keller notes many treat God like an employer: perform and keep performing in order to belong. That is unbiblical and spiritually dangerous, and it is what Paul corrects in Rome. It turns us into Pharisees; the teacher calls it his own struggle, like Martha refusing to sit at Jesus' feet. Nothing can earn our place; Jesus bore our sins and God counts His righteousness to us. Our belonging is anchored in His love, so what we do for God comes from gratitude: not sitting on the sidelines, which makes grace cheap, and not thinking our ministry earns our standing, which leads to pride, hypocrisy and Pharisaism.
- Study note (added): write down one thing you do for God that you secretly count on to make you belong. This week, do it once purely as thanks, and spend the same amount of time simply sitting with Romans 8:31-39.
